email.scenario: You recently signed up for a free sleep-hygiene workshop offered by a local health clinic. This morning you received a confirmation email, but it lists the workshop starting at 6:00 p.m. instead of the 5:00 p.m. time you selected, and the workshop is scheduled for tomorrow. Write an email to the clinic's workshop scheduling coordinator.
email.subject: Sleep-Hygiene Workshop Confirmation Time
bullets: Express appreciation for the clinic offering the free sleep-hygiene workshop.
Point out that the confirmation email lists 6:00 p.m. instead of the correct 5:00 p.m. start time.
Request a corrected confirmation before tomorrow's session.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: Long-distance rail operators are debating whether to require every passenger to hold an advance seat reservation, eliminating standing-room walk-up tickets during peak travel periods. Supporters argue reservations let operators plan capacity and guarantee every rider a seat, while critics worry that commuters who cannot book far ahead would lose access during the busiest hours. What do you think? Should reservations be mandatory for every passenger, or should operators keep offering walk-up tickets during peak periods? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Priya
studentPosts.post: I support mandatory reservations. Operators can only plan enough cars and staff if they know exactly how many passengers are coming. Standing-room ticket sales lead to an overcrowded platform and packed aisles during rush hour, which feels unsafe and makes the ride uncomfortable for everyone who paid for a seat.

studentPosts.name: Marcus
studentPosts.post: Requiring a reservation for every passenger would hurt commuters whose plans change at the last minute, like someone catching an earlier train after a meeting runs long. Walk-up tickets keep rail travel flexible and accessible. Overcrowding could be managed with more frequent trains instead of shutting spontaneous riders out entirely.
